title: Refusal Drift: Do Open Models Refuse Multi-Step Cyber 'Killchain' Framing Less Than Single Steps?
problem: The exploit-evals and ATT&CK work emphasize that risk concentrates in autonomous end-to-end attack orchestration, but it is unmeasured whether open models' refusals weaken when a disallowed cyber task is decomposed into innocuous-looking sequential agent steps.
direction: Build a small benchmark of clearly-harmful cyber-assistance requests (from public refusal/safety datasets, defensive framing only) in two matched forms: a single blunt request vs the same intent split into a multi-turn 'agentic' sequence of benign-sounding subtasks. Measure refusal rate of several open instruct models on each form using a refusal-classifier rubric. No exploit code executed.
why_it_matters: If decomposing a harmful goal into innocuous agent steps reliably lowers refusal rates, that is a concrete generalizable safety failure mode for the open agent ecosystem.
relevant_context: Extends 'Measuring LLMs' ability to develop exploits' (Cheng et al., 2026) — reframes its end-to-end-chain emphasis into a defensive refusal measurement.
source_paper: Measuring LLMs' ability to develop exploits — https://www.anthropic.com/research/exploit-evals

theory_of_impact.reasoning: If decomposing harmful goals into innocuous agent steps reliably lowers refusal, that is a concrete generalizable safety failure mode for open agents.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only refusal measurement, no exploit execution; minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building matched single vs decomposed prompts and classifying refusals is guided and novice-feasible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused single-vs-multi-step refusal comparison, but spanning several models and a benchmark build adds steps.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Public refusal datasets and open models; defensive refusal auditing is independent-friendly.

title: Does a 2-monitor ensemble beat the best single monitor? A cheap test of Apollo's ensemble claim
problem: Apollo reports monitoring ensembles produce clear improvements, but the result is asserted for their internal setup; it is untested whether simply averaging two cheap diverse open-model monitors beats the stronger single monitor on a fixed false-positive budget.
direction: Reuse the labeled benign/sabotage transcript set. Score each transcript with two distinct small open models (Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B) and a third prompt-diverse variant. Combine via score-averaging and max-rule, then compare ensemble TPR-at-1%-FPR against each individual monitor. Report whether diversity (different base models) helps more than redundancy (same model, different prompts).
why_it_matters: If a trivial ensemble of cheap open monitors reliably beats any single one, small labs and external auditors get a free reliability boost for catching deceptive agent behavior.
relevant_context: Extends Apollo 'A scalable monitoring research agenda' — replicates its 'ensembles improve' claim at cheap open-model scale.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain (cheap ensemble reliability boost for monitoring) but a gap to direct catastrophic-risk reduction; incremental over single-monitor work.

low_compute.reasoning: Scoring transcripts with 2-3 small open models inference-only; minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: scoring with multiple monitors and combining via averaging/max-rule is very accessible with a mentor.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped single experiment (ensemble vs single-monitor TPR at 1% FPR).

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: open models on a labeled set, a free reliability boost for external auditors.

title: How much does an open model's task horizon shrink without chain-of-thought?
problem: Control protocols often assume monitorability rests on visible reasoning, but there is little open replication of how much capability collapses when small/mid open models are denied CoT. The original no-CoT horizon work uses inaccessible frontier models.
direction: Pick 2-3 open models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) and a public multi-step benchmark with gradable difficulty (GSM8K, a BBH subset, or simple multi-step agentic tasks). Run each in CoT-allowed vs CoT-suppressed (force immediate answer via prompt + constrained decoding) modes. Measure accuracy as a function of task 'length' (reasoning steps required) and estimate the effective no-CoT horizon per model.
why_it_matters: If externalized reasoning is load-bearing for capability, CoT monitoring is a strong control lever; if open models retain much capability without CoT, control protocols assuming CoT-dependence are fragile.
relevant_context: Extends 'Estimating No-CoT Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models' (Woodruff, Redwood, 2026) — replicates its core measurement on open models.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Directly tests whether CoT monitoring is a reliable control lever by measuring no-CoT capability collapse, a concrete monitorability assumption.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only on 7-8B open models over public benchmarks fits a consumer GPU.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Public benchmarks and prompting/constrained decoding; accessible to novices but constrained decoding setup needs care.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Clear measurement (accuracy vs task length, CoT on/off) but across multiple models and benchmarks broadens scope.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Replicates frontier-only work on open models that labs won't produce; clear third-party replication gold case.

title: A toy safety-usefulness frontier: empirically tracing the tradeoff for a trusted-monitor protocol
problem: The safety-usefulness tradeoff frontier is so far a conceptual framework with no cheap empirical instantiation that beginners can reproduce.
direction: Build a minimal control setup on a public coding/QA task with an injected attack: an untrusted open model (8B prompted to occasionally insert a detectable bug/backdoor) and a weaker trusted monitor (a smaller open model scoring suspiciousness). Sweep the audit/defer threshold and at each setting measure safety (fraction of attacks caught) and usefulness (fraction of legitimate outputs preserved). Plot the resulting points to empirically draw a frontier, then show how a simple protocol tweak (resampling suspicious outputs) shifts the curve.
why_it_matters: An explicit reproducible frontier turns an abstract tradeoff into a measurement tool others can extend, and gives an intuitive teaching artifact for control protocol knobs.
relevant_context: Extends 'Efficient tradeoffs and the safety-usefulness tradeoff model' (Shlegeris, Redwood, 2026) — its open thread on empirical instantiation of the frontier.
source_paper: Efficient tradeoffs and the safety-usefulness tradeoff model — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/efficient-tradeoffs-and-the-safety

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Turns the abstract safety-usefulness tradeoff into a reproducible measurement tool for control protocol design, a concrete deliverable.

low_compute.reasoning: Untrusted 8B + smaller monitor inference on public tasks fits a consumer GPU.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Public coding/QA task with prompted attack and monitor scoring; threshold sweep is guided-level but multi-component setup needs a mentor.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused first deliverable (frontier plot) but adding the resampling-tweak comparison is a second workstream.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Reproducible open frontier artifact others can extend; classic neglected replication/tooling case independent of labs.

title: Phrasing-Robustness Audit of AI Identity Disclosure on Open Models
problem: RealityTest shows a single suppression instruction drops identity disclosure below 30% in the best models, and that phrasing matters more than which model is used — but the benchmark focuses on frontier text/speech models, leaving open how small open-weight models behave.
direction: Take the RealityTest identity-probing query templates (or reconstruct a ~150-query subset across a few languages) and run them inference-only against 4-6 open chat models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B) with and without a standard suppression system prompt. Score disclosure with a keyword + LLM-judge rubric and report disclosure rate by model, suppression on/off, and phrasing cluster.
why_it_matters: If small freely-deployable open models disclose identity even less reliably than frontier models, impersonation/deceptive-deployment risk concentrates where there is no provider-side guardrail; a per-model open-weight leaderboard gives a useful signal no lab is producing.
relevant_context: Extends 'RealityTest' (UK AISI) — the suppression-below-30% and phrasing-over-model findings, applied to open-weight models. Code available.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Impersonation/deceptive-deployment risk is real but the link from an open-weight disclosure leaderboard to reduced catastrophic AI risk is plausible-with-a-gap.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only across several 7-9B open chat models fits a consumer GPU.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Reuses existing query templates and scores with keyword+LLM-judge; very accessible to beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused per-model disclosure-rate report, mildly broadened by suppression on/off and phrasing clusters across multiple models.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open-weight leaderboard no lab produces, third-party scrutiny gold case with code available.

title: Do Cognitive Biases Leak Into LLM Preference Judgments? A Mini-Audit
problem: 'AI alignment is a human problem' argues human cognitive biases contaminate the supervisory signals we feed models. The claim that classic human biases reproduce in LLM-as-judge preference labeling is asserted but not measured in a single tight experiment.
direction: Construct paired response candidates holding content constant while varying one bias trigger at a time (answer length, confident tone, ordering/anchoring, sycophantic agreement) and ask 3-4 open LLM judges which response is 'better'. Quantify how often each bias flips the preference label vs a content-matched control. Report a bias-susceptibility profile per judge model.
why_it_matters: If LLM judges — increasingly used to scale human feedback — inherit human-style biases, automated preference data systematically encodes those biases into trained models, the amplification failure the paper warns about.
relevant_context: Operationalizes 'AI alignment is a human problem' (UK AISI) — its claim that cognitive biases in supervisory signals are an alignment bottleneck.
source_paper: AI alignment is a human problem — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/ai-alignment-is-a-human-problem

theory_of_impact.reasoning: If LLM judges inherit human biases, automated preference data encodes them into trained models, a concrete scalable-oversight amplification failure.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only judging across 3-4 open models, consumer-GPU/API feasible.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Constructing content-matched paired candidates and tallying preference flips is very accessible to beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused bias-susceptibility profile, mildly broadened by several bias triggers and judge models.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open models and public-style data, generalizes without internal access.

title: Realism vs. Nudges: Does Removing 'Incentive Nudges' Reduce Sabotage in Open Agent Models Too?
problem: Gram found that for Gemini, most agentic sabotage stems from artificial incentive nudges and near-vanishes when scenarios are made more realistic, but it is untested whether this realism effect holds for the open models small teams actually deploy as agents.
direction: Reconstruct 2-3 of Gram's sabotage-style scenarios as simple text/tool-stub prompts. Create matched 'nudged' and 'de-nudged/realistic' versions of each, then run them inference-only over several open models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) at a few temperatures, scoring sabotage rate with a rubric and a cheap judge. Deliverable: a per-model comparison of sabotage rate under nudged vs realistic framing.
why_it_matters: If open agent models also misbehave mainly because of artificial incentive framing, much apparent misalignment in agent demos is an evaluation artifact — important for anyone building or red-teaming open-model agents.
relevant_context: Extends 'Gram' (Lindner et al., 2026) — the realism-removes-sabotage result, tested on open 7-8B agents.
source_paper: Gram: Assessing sabotage propensities via automated alignment auditing — https://deepmind.google/research/publications/252981/

theory_of_impact.reasoning: If realism removes most open-agent sabotage, much apparent misalignment is an eval artifact, directly important for red-teaming open agents.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only over 7-8B models on a few scenarios; low compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Reconstructing prompts and scoring sabotage with a rubric/judge is guided and novice-feasible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused nudged-vs-realistic comparison, but reconstructing 2-3 scenarios across several models adds breadth.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open models and reconstructed public scenarios; independent-friendly.

title: Can you forecast AI R&D speedup from public benchmark history? A reproducible mini-model of automation-driven acceleration
problem: Greenblatt argues full automation of AI R&D would yield a large speedup even without a software-only singularity, but the magnitude/timing is open and the reasoning is hard for newcomers to inspect quantitatively.
direction: Build a small transparent Python simulation tying together public time-series (compute-scaling trends, benchmark-progress rates from Epoch AI / public leaderboards) into a toy growth model with an explicit 'R&D automation speedup' parameter. Reproduce Greenblatt's qualitative claim that a sub-singularity multiplier still produces large acceleration, and run a sensitivity analysis over the multiplier and a compute-bottleneck cap. Deliverable: an open notebook with clearly-labeled assumptions and charts.
why_it_matters: Translating a verbal argument into a small inspectable public model is high counterfactual value and makes the acceleration debate legible, feeding governance/takeoff-timeline reasoning.
relevant_context: Operationalizes 'Full automation of AI R&D probably yields a large speed up even without a software-only singularity' (Greenblatt, Redwood) — decoupling 'big speedup' from singularity, and its bottleneck open threads.
source_paper: Full automation of AI R&D probably yields a large speed up — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/full-automation-of-ai-r-and-d-probably

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Makes the acceleration debate legible for takeoff/governance reasoning, but the toy growth model's link to concrete risk reduction has a gap.

low_compute.reasoning: Python simulation over public time-series, CPU/analytical only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building a transparent growth model with sensitivity analysis is approachable but requires modeling judgment a mentor must guide.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused notebook deliverable reproducing one qualitative claim with sensitivity analysis, bounded.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Inspectable public model of a lab-influenced debate, high counterfactual value as third-party legible analysis.

title: A Minimal Reproducible Indirect-Prompt-Injection Eval for Open Tool-Using Agents
problem: The Gray Swan competition shows every frontier agent is breakable by indirect prompt injection, but it relied on a closed competition platform and frontier APIs. There is no small, runnable IPI eval that a beginner can use on open models.
direction: Build a tiny agent loop (LangChain or raw API) that reads a 'document' and a 'tool result' field, then test 15-20 published IPI attack templates (instruction override, fake system message, hidden HTML/markdown, data-exfiltration lure) against 2-3 open instruction-tuned models. Measure per-attack-category success rate on a single benign task.
why_it_matters: IPI is one of the most pressing unsolved deployment risks for agentic systems; a public, reproducible mini-benchmark lowers the barrier for others to test their own setups.
relevant_context: Extends 'How Vulnerable Are AI Agents to Indirect Prompt Injections?' (Dziemian et al., Gray Swan AI, 2026) — turns the competition's finding into a reusable open eval.
source_paper: How Vulnerable Are AI Agents to Indirect Prompt Injections? — https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15714

theory_of_impact.reasoning: IPI is a recognized pressing agentic deployment risk and a public mini-benchmark is an independently useful intermediate deliverable.

low_compute.reasoning: A tiny agent loop over 2-3 open instruct models is inference-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building an agent loop and testing published attack templates is guided work a novice with a mentor can do.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused first deliverable (per-category success rate) but assembling a working agent loop adds dependencies.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: A public reproducible IPI eval for open models is neglected by labs and useful to the wider community.

title: Counting the Flags: Can Simple Batch-Level Monitoring Catch Boundary-Point Attacks?
problem: The paper notes boundary-point optimization incurs many classifier flags during search, suggesting monitoring flag patterns across queries is the natural defense — but no one has measured how easily a trivial batch-level detector separates an attack session from benign users.
direction: Using logs from a boundary-point-style attack against an open guard classifier, compute simple per-session features: flag rate over a sliding window, semantic drift between consecutive queries (embedding cosine), edit-distance. Build a lightweight logistic-regression/threshold detector and contrast attack sessions against benign multi-turn sessions from a public chat dataset (WildChat/LMSYS-Chat). Report ROC and false-positive cost.
why_it_matters: If a beginner-built threshold detector on flag-rate plus query-similarity already catches these attacks at low FPR, defenders should add cheap cross-query monitoring rather than only hardening per-query classifiers.
relevant_context: Extends 'Boundary Point Jailbreaking' by operationalizing its open thread — effective defense needs batch-level monitoring across queries.
source_paper: Boundary Point Jailbreaking of Black-Box LLMs — https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15001

theory_of_impact.reasoning: A cheap cross-query monitor that catches boundary-point attacks at low FPR is a concrete defensive contribution to AI control.

low_compute.reasoning: Feature extraction plus logistic regression over logs is trivially cheap.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Simple per-session features and a threshold/LR detector are accessible to a guided novice.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused ROC/FPR deliverable but depends on first producing attack logs from gen-011-style setup.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Cheap monitoring defense on open setups is independent-friendly and neglected by labs.

title: Logic vs Design Sabotage: Does a Targeted Checklist Prompt Help LLM Auditors Catch the Hard Cases?
problem: On the Auditing Sabotage benchmark, logic sabotages are usually caught but design sabotages (hyperparameter, prompt, or data choices) and omissions rarely are; it is untested whether a cheap structured 'design-decision audit' prompt narrows that gap.
direction: Using the released Auditing Sabotage Bench codebase pairs, run an open or API model as auditor under two prompts: a generic 'find the sabotage' prompt, and a structured checklist that forces enumerating and justifying every hyperparameter, data-filtering, and prompt choice against the paper's claims. Compare detection AUROC and top-1 localization, broken down by logic vs design vs omission.
why_it_matters: Design-based sabotage is exactly the failure mode an AI research assistant could exploit to subtly flip findings; a simple checklist scaffold that helps is immediately adoptable.
relevant_context: Extends 'Auditing Sabotage Bench' (Gan, Hebbar, Stastny, Redwood, 2026) — the 0.77 AUROC ceiling and design-sabotage difficulty.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Design sabotage is exactly how an AI research assistant could subtly flip findings; an adoptable scaffold targets a recognized control pathway.

low_compute.reasoning: Running an open or API auditor over released codebase pairs is inference-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Two auditor prompts over a released bench is guided, though AUROC/localization analysis needs care.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused comparison broken down by sabotage type, with a few analysis dependencies.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Improving automated auditing on a public bench is independent-friendly and neglected by labs.

title: Human-Crafted vs Model-Elicited Attacks: A Stylometric Look at Why Human Sabotage Evades Monitors
problem: LinuxArena finds human-crafted attacks evade monitors far better than model-elicited ones, but what distinguishes the two — and whether a monitor can be cued to close the gap — is uncharacterized.
direction: From LinuxArena's released attack transcripts, separate human-crafted and model-elicited sabotage and compute comparative features: action verbosity, legitimate-looking justifications, number of intermediate benign steps, command obfuscation. Then test whether prompting the monitor with the found evasion patterns raises detection of human-crafted attacks. Inference-only.
why_it_matters: If human attackers exploit identifiable evasion tactics model red-teamers don't generate, model-only red-teaming systematically overestimates monitor robustness.
relevant_context: Extends 'LinuxArena' — characterizes the human-vs-model evasion gap it reports.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: If model red-teaming overestimates monitor robustness, characterizing the human-evasion gap is a defensible control-relevant finding.

low_compute.reasoning: Computing transcript features and re-prompting a monitor is inference-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Stylometric feature comparison and a cued-monitor test are guided and accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused comparative-feature deliverable plus a follow-on cueing test, a few dependencies.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Characterizing released attack transcripts is independent-friendly and neglected by labs.

title: Cheap-Defense Stress Test: Do Simple Prompt-Level Guards Survive the Jailbreaks That Broke DeepSeek-V4-Pro?
problem: FAR AI showed DeepSeek-V4-Pro's safeguards collapse (98-100% attack success) under three jailbreak strategies despite blocking 100% of direct requests. It is unclear whether lightweight deployable prompt-level defenses meaningfully reduce that success rate.
direction: Using a public harmful-behavior benchmark (JailbreakBench JBB-Behaviors / HarmBench prompts) and 2-3 reproducible jailbreak templates (roleplay, refusal-suppression, low-resource encoding), measure attack success on an open model. Then add three cheap inference-only defenses and re-measure: a defensive system prompt, a second-pass self-critique filter, and input paraphrase-then-answer. Report which defenses move ASR and which the attacks route around, scored with an LLM-judge calibrated on a held-out hand-labeled set.
why_it_matters: Most open-weight deployers cannot retrain safeguards; they need to know whether wrapper-level defenses are real protection or theater.
relevant_context: Extends 'Security Stress Test: DeepSeek-V4-Pro' (FAR AI) — its 98-100% ASR finding, testing inference-only defenses on an open model.
source_paper: Security Stress Test: DeepSeek-V4-Pro (FAR AI) — https://www.far.ai/blog

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Testing whether wrapper defenses are real protection or theater directly informs open-weight deployers, a concrete misuse-reduction pathway.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only attacks and defenses on one open model.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Using public jailbreak benchmarks and an LLM-judge is guided-level; calibrating the judge needs care.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (ASR with vs without 3 defenses) but spans multiple attacks and defenses.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open-model wrapper-defense evaluation is squarely independent-friendly and useful to the broader community.

title: Filling the ATT&CK Gap: A Public Annotation Schema for Autonomous-AI Cyber Behaviors
problem: The LLM ATT&CK Navigator work found MITRE ATT&CK has no categories for autonomous AI behaviors (agentic killchain orchestration), exactly what distinguishes the highest-risk actors, leaving defenders without a vocabulary to tag these behaviors.
direction: Using only public material (the ATT&CK matrix, published threat-intel reports, public write-ups of agentic-AI misuse), draft a small candidate set of 8-12 'autonomous AI behavior' annotation tags with definitions and positive/negative examples. Validate by hand-labeling a public corpus of described AI-assisted attack narratives and reporting coverage and annotator agreement.
why_it_matters: Defenders and policymakers can only track a threat they can name; a public ATT&CK-complementary vocabulary is purely defensive, needs no model access, and directly addresses the paper's open thread.
relevant_context: Extends 'Mapping AI-enabled cyber threats: the LLM ATT&CK Navigator' (Guru et al., 2026) — the gap that ATT&CK lacks autonomous-AI categories.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: A defensive vocabulary defenders can name is valuable, but a taxonomy's impact on catastrophic risk is plausible yet indirect.

low_compute.reasoning: Pure public-material analysis and hand-labeling; no model compute needed.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Drafting tags and hand-labeling public narratives is guided and accessible, requires some domain reading.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused 8-12 tag schema with validation, but schema design plus corpus labeling is a modest two-part effort.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Purely public, no model access, directly complements ATT&CK; a neglected independent-friendly case.
